summary: Specifies a TELNET option letting a client and server negotiate which character set and translation to use. It was experimental.

eli5.summary: Two people agree on which alphabet to write in before they chat, so letters do not get mixed up.

questions: how does telnet negotiate character sets
what is a telnet translation table
when should telnet use charset negotiation
subtitle: Letting TELNET clients and servers agree on what alphabet to use

tldr.problem: When TELNET users in different countries connect to servers, there is no standard way for the client and server to agree which alphabet or character set to use, leading to garbled or misunderstood text.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 2066 adds a CHARSET option to TELNET that lets either side propose a character set and the other side accept it, reject all proposals, or provide a translation table if it prefers a different set.
tldr.outcome: This was experimental and never became widely adopted, remaining as a specification for systems that need to handle multiple character sets in TELNET sessions.

today: RFC 2066 is Experimental and has never been adopted as a standard. It defined a working system but proved too complex for widespread use, and most TELNET implementations handle character sets through other means.

sections.title: The CHARSET Option for TELNET
sections.content:
TELNET is a text protocol that predates widespread international character support. RFC 2066 adds an optional mechanism called CHARSET that lets a TELNET client and server negotiate which character set (alphabet) to use for their session.

The option works by having either side propose a list of supported character sets in order of preference, with the other side accepting one, rejecting all of them, or offering a translation table to convert between incompatible sets.
sections.eli5: Before chatting, one person suggests their alphabet, and the other says yes, no, or offers to translate.

sections.title: How Character Sets Are Negotiated
sections.content:
TELNET negotiation always starts with the standard WILL/DO messages that activate the CHARSET option on both sides. Once both sides agree the option is available, either one can send a CHARSET REQUEST message listing one or more character sets it wants to use.

The receiver responds with one of four replies: ACCEPTED (picking one of the proposed sets), REJECTED (unable to handle any of them), TTABLE-IS (sending a translation table to use a different set), or another REQUEST if both sent one at the same time (in which case the server rejects the client and the client must respond to the server's request).
sections.eli5: One side suggests alphabets. The other picks one, says no, or says 'I will translate between yours and mine.'

sections.title: Translation Tables Between Character Sets
sections.content:
When the RFC mentions TTABLE (translation table), it means a pair of lookup tables that map characters from one set to another. Each TTABLE-IS message carries two tables: one mapping forward from the requested set to the preferred set, and one mapping backward.

The translation works by using a character's numeric value as an index into the table. If a character has no mapping entry in the table, it passes through unchanged. This mechanism allows a client and server with incompatible character sets to still communicate.
sections.eli5: A translation table is like a dictionary: 'A in your alphabet is this character in my alphabet,' and back again.

sections.title: Modes and Constraints
sections.content:
Character set translation only happens in BINARY mode (RFC 856). In normal TELNET mode, all data is assumed to be NVT ASCII, the standard text representation. The CHARSET option should be used with the END-OF-RECORD option (RFC 885) on block-mode terminals so both sides are clear about record boundaries.

At any point during a session, either side can initiate a new CHARSET negotiation, but only one negotiation can be active at a time. If a side receives a new CHARSET REQUEST while another is in progress, it must reject it. The RFC names two early uses: the Internet Name Server and the Trivial File Transfer Protocol.
sections.eli5: It only works when TELNET is in binary mode, and you have to finish one alphabet agreement before starting another.

sections.title: Experimental Status
sections.content:
RFC 2066 is experimental and was never advanced to standard status. It specified a working system but came at a time when character set support was becoming complex, and the RFC included optional support for translation tables that many implementations did not add.

Systems that needed to handle multiple TELNET sessions with different character sets often used other methods instead, such as the BINARY option with local conventions or terminal type negotiation.
sections.eli5: This was an experiment that sounded good but was never adopted widely because other methods were simpler.
